paragraphs.title: The Lot and the Southern Boundary

easy.question: Who received the lot according to the verse?
answers: the tribe of the children of Judah
easy.explanation: The verse says the lot was for the tribe of the children of Judah.

easy.question: To which boundary does the verse say the border reaches?
easy.explanation: The verse mentions the border reaching 'unto the border of Edom'.

easy.question: Which direction does the phrase 'the bay that looketh southward' indicate?
easy.explanation: The phrase specifies the bay looks southward, i.e., toward the south.

medium.question: Which geographic feature is named in verse 2 as the boundary of the inheritance?
medium.explanation: Verse 2 refers to 'the shore of the salt sea', meaning the Dead Sea.

medium.question: In the phrase 'the lot of the tribe' (v.1), what does 'lot' most likely mean in this context?
medium.explanation: Here 'lot' refers to the allotment or assignment of land to the tribe, not luck or punishment.

medium.question: What does the Hebrew literary phrase rendered 'the uttermost part of the south coast' imply about 'Maalehacrabbim'?
answers: a southern extreme point of the territory
medium.explanation: The wording indicates a southern extreme point — the farthest part of the southern coast.

challenge.question: In the phrase 'the bay that looketh southward' (v.2), what geographic feature is suggested by 'bay' or 'point' of the coast?
answers: a protruding tongue of land facing south
challenge.explanation: In ancient geographic language a 'bay' or 'point' often denotes a tongue or spur of land projecting toward the south.

challenge.question: What is the historical implication of mentioning the border as reaching to Edom for Judah's inheritance?
answers: that it marked an administrative separation from another people (Edom)
that it corresponds to modern national borders only
challenge.explanation: Mentioning Edom marks a frontier or separation from the territory of another people, not direct rule over them.

challenge.question: What does 'the shore of the salt sea' imply about the location of the boundary?
answers: that the border did not reach any sea
that the border reached the Mediterranean coast
that the border reached the shore of the Dead Sea
challenge.explanation: The phrase specifies the Salt Sea (Dead Sea), so the border reached that shore.

paragraphs.title: Boundary Route from South to North

easy.question: When the verse says 'and it went out to the south', which direction is indicated?
easy.explanation: The phrase indicates movement toward the south.

easy.question: Which place does the border reach after passing Zin, according to the verse?
easy.explanation: The verse notes it passed Zin and ascended to Kadesh Barnea next.

easy.question: Which sea is mentioned in verse 5 as part of the border?
easy.explanation: Verse 5 mentions 'the Salt Sea' as a boundary.

medium.question: According to the verses, where do 'the goings out of that coast' end?
medium.explanation: The text says the goings out of the coast were at the sea — the border reached the sea.

medium.question: In 'the goings out of that coast were at the sea' (v.4), what does 'goings out' most likely mean?
answers: points where the coast meets the sea
medium.explanation: Here 'goings out' refers to the points where the coastline or coastal boundary meets the sea.

medium.question: What is meant by 'the north side of Betharabah, and the stone of Bohan the son of Reuben' in the listing of the boundary?
answers: a personal name marking a boundary stone
the name of a mountain range
medium.explanation: The stone named for Bohan son of Reuben functions as a named boundary marker.

challenge.question: In 'and fetched a compass to Karkaa' (v.3), what does the phrase 'fetched a compass' mean in geographical terms?
challenge.explanation: The phrase indicates moving around or drawing a circuit/compass around a place — i.e., to encircle or skirt it.

challenge.question: What does the mention of 'the River of Egypt' (Nahal Mitzrayim) at the coast imply historically/geographically?
answers: it marks the Egyptian frontier, often identified with Wadi el-Arish
challenge.explanation: Traditionally 'River of Egypt' in boundary descriptions is identified with the Wadi el-Arish region marking the southern frontier with Egypt.

challenge.question: What does the verb sense in 'and fetched a compass' tell us about how the boundary runs around the land?
answers: that it rounds or skirts the territory
challenge.explanation: The wording conveys that the boundary rounds or skirts the territory in a curving or circuitous path.

easy.question: What is the main subject described in these verses (Joshua 15:7–11)?
answers: a description of maritime trade routes
easy.explanation: These verses detail points and the movement of the boundary — a territorial description.

easy.question: Which city is identified in the passage as the 'Jebusite's shoulder' and named explicitly?
easy.explanation: The passage refers to the Jebusite area — identified as Jerusalem in the verse.

easy.question: What is noted about 'the waters of En-shemesh' in verse 7?
answers: they are used as a boundary marker (the border reaches them)
it is the name of a coastal city
it is the name of a person
easy.explanation: The verse says the border passed to the waters of En-shemesh, using the spring as a reference point.

medium.question: In 'the goings out thereof were at Enrogel' (v.7), what does 'goings out' most likely refer to?
answers: branches of waters or water outlets
the name of a further town
medium.explanation: Within a water context, 'goings out' refers to the outlets or flows of the spring's water.

medium.question: What geographic mix do most of the named locations in this sequence represent?
answers: a mixture of springs, towns and hills — varied geographic features
medium.explanation: The verses mention springs, towns and hills, showing a mix of geographic elements.

medium.question: What can be inferred about Jerusalem's status from being called 'the Jebusite's shoulder' in this passage?
answers: that it still belonged to the Jebusites and was not fully in Judah's hands then
that it was already Judah's capital
that it is mentioned only as a geometric point with no political meaning
medium.explanation: Calling it 'Jebusite' suggests it remained in Jebusite hands at that time, not fully under Judah's control.

challenge.question: In 'the goings out thereof were at Enrogel' (v.7), what does the phrase indicate about Enrogel's role?
answers: that Enrogel was primarily a market town
that Enrogel functioned as a point where water flowed out (a landmark)
that Enrogel was a mountain stronghold
challenge.explanation: The phrase shows Enrogel served as a landmark tied to water outlets — a notable reference point for the border.

challenge.question: What common feature do many of these boundary reference points share?
answers: they are all written as agricultural laws
they are a mixture of springs, towns and hills used as landmarks
challenge.explanation: They mix natural springs with towns and hilltops — typical kinds of landmarks for ancient boundaries.

challenge.question: What does the final phrase 'and the goings out of the border were to the sea' (v.11) imply about the border's extent?
answers: that the border ended inland only
that the boundary reached toward the sea (westward)
that the phrase names a person 'Yamah'
challenge.explanation: It indicates the boundary extended to or toward the sea — i.e., westward to the coast.

easy.question: Which tribe is described in this verse as having the coast to the great sea?
easy.explanation: The verse explicitly names the coast of the children of Judah.

easy.question: What body of water is meant by 'the great sea' in this verse?
easy.explanation: 'The great sea' or 'the great sea' generally refers to the Mediterranean Sea in this context.

easy.question: What does the simple phrase 'round about according to their families' mean here?
answers: the border was only outside the towns
the border was recorded only for paperwork
the border was set around family holdings — surrounding households
easy.explanation: It indicates the border was set surrounding the family parcels — the allotments were allocated by family.

medium.question: Why does the verse reiterate 'This is the coast of the children of Judah' after mentioning the sea?
answers: to list specific cities on the coast
to define explicitly that this coastline is the boundary of the tribe of Judah
medium.explanation: The repetition clarifies that the described coastline is indeed the boundary of Judah's territory.

medium.question: In the phrase 'round about according to their families' (v.12), what does 'round about' mean?
medium.explanation: 'Round about' means surrounding or encompassing the family holdings.

medium.question: What does the term 'coast'/'border' refer to in this context of land division?
answers: a line defining divisions between families and tribes
medium.explanation: It denotes a territorial dividing line that defines the allotment of land among families and tribes.

challenge.question: Which modern sea most closely corresponds to the 'the great sea' mentioned here?
challenge.explanation: In biblical usage 'the great sea' commonly refers to the Mediterranean Sea.

challenge.question: What social-administrative meaning does 'according to their families' have for land allotment?
answers: land was organized and distributed by families/tribes
the families were required to go to sea for trade
challenge.explanation: It indicates land was allocated according to family/tribal units — an organized tribal allotment system.

challenge.question: Why does the text double back to state 'this is the coast of the children of Judah' — what does that kind of repetition usually indicate in biblical style?
answers: a later translator added the line
an emphasis and clarification that the described line is indeed Judah's boundary
challenge.explanation: Such repetition is typically used for emphasis and precision: to make clear that the mentioned line is the official border of Judah.

easy.question: Which city was given to Caleb according to verse 13?
easy.explanation: Verse 13 states that the city of Arba (father of Anak) is Hebron, given to Caleb.

easy.question: Which three sons of Anak did Caleb drive out (v.14)?
easy.explanation: Verse 14 names Sheshai, Ahiman and Talmai as the sons of Anak Caleb drove out.

easy.question: Who captured Kirjathsepher and received Achsah in marriage (v.17)?
easy.explanation: Othniel, Caleb's brother, took the city and Caleb gave him Achsah as wife.

medium.question: What incentive did Caleb offer to whoever captured Kirjathsepher (v.16)?
medium.explanation: Caleb promised his daughter Achsah to the man who captured Kirjathsepher.

medium.question: In 'the upper springs, and the nether springs' (v.19), what are 'springs' referring to?
medium.explanation: The terms indicate sources or reservoirs of water — upper and lower springs/wells.

medium.question: Why did Achsah ask her father for springs of water after marrying Othniel (v.19)?
answers: she wanted to flee the town
she had been given a southern land and needed water sources
she wanted to raise only flocks
medium.explanation: She requested water because she had been given land in the south, so water sources were necessary for the inheritance.

challenge.question: What is the significance of granting 'the upper springs and the nether springs' to Achsah?
answers: it gave her a trading post
it gave her only a single water source
it provided water sources at two elevations or locations
challenge.explanation: The wording indicates she received water sources in both higher and lower locations — two distinct sources.

challenge.question: What does verse 20 'This is the inheritance of the tribe of the children of Judah according to their families' denote?
answers: a description only of Caleb's land
a listing of Caleb's private holdings, separate from Judah
a designation that these listings are part of Judah's tribal inheritance
challenge.explanation: The verse summarizes that the described lands form part of the tribe of Judah's inheritance by family.

challenge.question: What did Achsah do when she came to Caleb according to verses 18–19?
answers: seized a field from her father by force
persuaded her father to grant a piece of land and water sources for them
refused to speak with her father
challenge.explanation: The text says she urged him to ask her father for a field; she prompted the request that secured springs for her.

paragraphs.title: Cities of the Tribe of Judah

easy.question: Which tribe is the list in these verses associated with?
easy.explanation: The passage begins 'the uttermost cities of the tribe of the children of Judah'.

easy.question: To which boundary do the listed cities reach?
answers: to the border of Edom in the south
to the Jordan River in the east
to the sea in the west
easy.explanation: Verse 21 states these cities are toward the border of Edom in the Negev (south).

easy.question: Which of the following names appears among verses 21–30?
easy.explanation: Kabzeel (Kabzeel) is listed in verse 21; Samaria and Jerusalem are not in this list.

medium.question: Which of the following does NOT appear in the list (vv.21–30)?
medium.explanation: Kedesh and Baalah are in the list; Bethlehem does not appear in these verses.

medium.question: In 'unto the border of Edom' (v.21), what does the word 'border' indicate?
medium.explanation: 'Border' here means a territorial dividing line — the edge of Judah's allotment.

medium.question: Which verse lists Kinah, Dimonah and Adadah?
medium.explanation: Verse 22 names Kinah, Dimonah and Adadah.

challenge.question: Which statement about Hazor in this list is correct?
answers: Hazor is not mentioned at all
Hazor is mentioned more than once
challenge.explanation: The name Hazor appears in multiple places in the list, so it is mentioned more than once.

challenge.question: In what general geographic area are the cities named in these verses mainly located?
challenge.explanation: The passage indicates these cities are at the southern end of Judah's territory — in the Negev.

challenge.question: What is the likely purpose of listing these towns in Joshua?
answers: to record battle plans for each city
to document ritual practices held there
to define territorial boundaries and tribal allotments
challenge.explanation: Joshua contains lists of towns to document the tribal allotments and boundaries; this listing maps Judah's towns.

easy.question: Which of these towns appears in verse 31?
easy.explanation: Verse 31 lists Ziklag at the head of the sequence.

easy.question: What number is given in verse 32 for all the towns listed there?
easy.explanation: The verse states 'all the cities twenty and nine' — 29 towns total.

easy.question: What do these verses primarily do?
easy.explanation: These verses are a list of town names belonging to Judah.

medium.question: What does 'their villages' mean in the phrase 'all the cities twenty and nine, with their villages'?
answers: small dependent settlements or hamlets around the towns
medium.explanation: 'Their villages' refers to dependent settlements or hamlets tied to the towns.

medium.question: To which tribal inheritance do the towns in this section belong?
medium.explanation: Joshua 15 concerns the inheritance of the tribe of Judah, and these towns are part of that allotment.

medium.question: What does the summary 'all the cities twenty and nine' indicate about the list that precedes it?
answers: that the names are part of a larger census of people
that it is a segment of a comprehensive count of towns in the area
that the number twenty-nine refers only to the villages
medium.explanation: The phrase summarizes that the preceding named towns total 29 — part of the regional town count.

challenge.question: Which town mentioned here later appears in the story of David in 1 Samuel?
challenge.explanation: Ziklag is known from the David narratives in 1 Samuel as a place associated with him.

challenge.question: What common geographic feature do most of these towns share?
answers: they are in the far north (Galilee)
they are in the south/Negev region
they are on the Mediterranean coast
challenge.explanation: Many of these towns are located in the southern part of Judah's allotment — the Negev area.

challenge.question: Which of the following place-names in this passage is also the name of a familiar fruit?
challenge.explanation: Rimmon is also the Hebrew word for pomegranate, a common fruit; here it is the name of a town.

paragraphs.title: The Shephelah: Towns of the Lowland

easy.question: Which of the following towns appears in verses 33–36?
easy.explanation: Zorah (Tsoreah) is listed in verse 33. Jericho and Shechem are not in this segment.

easy.question: What number is given in verse 36 for the towns listed in this section?
easy.explanation: Verse 36 states 'fourteen cities with their villages' — 14 towns.

easy.question: How does verse 36 end the list?
answers: with a list of rivers and borders
with a count: 'fourteen cities with their villages'
easy.explanation: The verse concludes by tallying the fourteen towns and noting their villages.

medium.question: In 'And in the valley, Eshtaol...' (v.33), what does 'valley' (the Shephelah) refer to?
answers: a lowland plain between the hills
medium.explanation: The Shephelah denotes the lowland plain region between the Judean hills and the coastal plain.

medium.question: What is the character of this section of the chapter, based on the words used?
answers: a list of settlements in the Shephelah region
medium.explanation: The text mainly lists towns and villages — it is a catalogue of settlements in the lowland.

medium.question: What does the closing phrase 'and their villages' add to the list of towns?
answers: that each town was an isolated castle
that the list also includes the smaller dependent settlements around the towns
that the towns had no surrounding lands
medium.explanation: The phrase shows the listing includes both the towns and the smaller villages or hamlets associated with them.

challenge.question: Why might two similar names like 'Gederah' and 'Gederothaim' both appear in the list?
answers: they are dialectal variants of the same place
they represent two distinct settlements with related names
they are scribal corruptions with no meaning
challenge.explanation: Ancient lists often record two distinct settlements that have related names; they are treated as separate places.

challenge.question: What does noting 'their villages' tell us about settlement patterns?
answers: that each town was usually accompanied by smaller dependent hamlets
that every town was a military post only
that everyone lived isolated on farms only
challenge.explanation: It implies towns functioned as centers with associated villages and agricultural holdings around them.

challenge.question: Which pair of names appears together in verses 33–36?
challenge.explanation: Jarmuth and Adullam (Adullam) are listed together in this group (v.34); the other pairs are not.

easy.question: What do verses 37–41 mainly list?
easy.explanation: These verses provide a list of towns and settlements in Judah's territory.

easy.question: Which of these town names appears in this passage?
easy.explanation: Kabbon is listed in the passage; Ein Gedi and Jerusalem are elsewhere.

easy.question: What number of towns is given in verse 41 for this group?
easy.explanation: Verse 41 states 'sixteen cities with their villages' — sixteen towns.

medium.question: What does the place-name element 'Mizpeh' suggest about such a site (v.38)?
medium.explanation: Mizpeh generally denotes a lookout or watch-site — a place of observation.

medium.question: What does the phrase 'sixteen cities with their villages' (v.41) indicate about the list?
answers: that each city had multiple administrative districts listed separately
that there were sixteen main towns plus their surrounding dependent villages
that only the villages are counted
medium.explanation: It shows the list includes sixteen principal towns along with the smaller settlements attached to them.

medium.question: What is the main type of items enumerated in verses 37–41?
medium.explanation: The items are place-names — towns and their associated villages.

challenge.question: What does the presence of names like 'Migdal-gad' and 'Mizpeh' suggest about the area's topography?
answers: that it was entirely flat with no vantage points
that it included heights and lookout points (towers or hills)
that it was a coastal island zone
challenge.explanation: Names meaning 'tower' or 'lookout' imply spots of elevation or fortification used for observation.

challenge.question: In the context of Joshua, where are these towns most likely located geographically?
answers: in the southern desert far from Judah
challenge.explanation: These names are listed in the section describing Judah's territory, typically in the Shephelah and surrounding lowlands.

challenge.question: What does the term 'their villages' (v.41) imply for interpreting the list?
answers: that the cities were only ceremonial centers
that each city had surrounding villages or farmsteads — the towns were centers of a wider settlement pattern
challenge.explanation: 'Their villages' indicates the towns were accompanied by satellite hamlets and agricultural lands, not isolated urban centers.

paragraphs.title: Libnah, Keilah and the Central Area

easy.question: How many names are in verse 42 ('Libnah, Ether, and Ashan')?
easy.explanation: Verse 42 lists three place-names: Libnah, Ether and Ashan.

easy.question: Which of the following names appears in verses 42–44?
easy.explanation: Libnah is mentioned in verse 42; Shiloh and Jericho are not part of this short section.

easy.question: What do the names in verses 42–44 have in common?
easy.explanation: They are place-names — towns and settlements within Judah's allotment.

medium.question: In 'nine cities and their villages' (v.44), what does the term 'their villages' refer to?
answers: small dependent settlements or farmsteads attached to the towns
the number of residents in the town
medium.explanation: It denotes smaller settlements or hamlets associated with each named town, not courts or population counts.

medium.question: What does the phrase 'nine cities' (v.44) function as in the list?
answers: a numerical count of how many towns are in that group
medium.explanation: 'Nine cities' succinctly indicates the number of towns listed in that subsection.

medium.question: What general purpose do these enumerations of towns and their villages serve in the chapter?
answers: to show settlement distribution and the territorial allotment to Judah
to list the winners of a contest
medium.explanation: They document the towns comprising Judah's territorial allotment and settlement pattern.

challenge.question: What can be inferred about towns described as 'cities and their villages' in this chapter?
answers: that they were only military posts
that these towns served as centers surrounded by dependent agricultural villages
that these were seasonal camps only
challenge.explanation: The formula implies an urban center with surrounding smaller settlements and agricultural holdings.

challenge.question: Why might the author add 'and their villages' instead of listing every small settlement individually?
answers: to emphasize that each city had accompanying rural communities without naming each one
to indicate each city had a temple only
to show the towns were uninhabited
challenge.explanation: The phrase summarizes the existence of satellite settlements without enumerating every minor hamlet, making the list manageable.

challenge.question: What overall conclusion about the chapter can be drawn from its many town lists?
answers: that it is a military chronicle only
that it aims to register the distribution of land and towns assigned to Judah
that it is a poetic composition with no geographic value
challenge.explanation: The repeated lists serve to record the allotment of towns and lands belonging to the tribe of Judah.

paragraphs.title: Ekron, Ashdod and the Sea Border

easy.question: Which towns are named in these verses (45–47)?
easy.explanation: Verses 45–47 mention Ekron, Ashdod and Gaza and their towns and villages.

easy.question: What is said about Ekron in verse 45?
answers: it and its daughters and villages are listed
that it is the capital city
easy.explanation: The verse mentions Ekron together with her towns and villages — including dependent settlements.

easy.question: Which sea is associated with the boundary in these verses?
easy.explanation: The coast reaches the 'great sea', i.e., the Mediterranean.

medium.question: What ordering appears in the list of towns in these verses (which comes first)?
medium.explanation: The passage lists Ekron first, then areas near Ashdod, then Ashdod and Gaza.

medium.question: In 'unto the river of Egypt, and the great sea, and the border thereof' (v.46), what does 'border' mean?
medium.explanation: Here 'border' means the territorial limit — the boundary line of the land.

medium.question: How far south does the passage extend according to these verses?
answers: to the River of Egypt (often identified with Wadi el-Arish)
medium.explanation: The text states the coastal boundary extends 'unto the river of Egypt', traditionally identified with Wadi el-Arish.

challenge.question: Why does the phrase 'and her towns and her villages' recur after each major town name?
answers: to list separate administrative units not connected to the town
to emphasize the town together with its dependent settlements (villages and hamlets)
challenge.explanation: The phrase systematically includes both the main town and its dependent settlements, clarifying the full extent of the town's domain.

challenge.question: Which modern feature is commonly identified with the biblical 'river of Egypt' in many geographical traditions?
challenge.explanation: Many commentators identify the biblical 'river of Egypt' with Wadi el-Arish at the Sinai frontier, not the Nile.

challenge.question: What does the clause 'from Ekron even unto the sea' (v.46) indicate about Ekron's territorial reach?
answers: that Ekron's domain extended down to the coast
that Ekron was far inland with no sea access
that Ekron sat on an island
challenge.explanation: The phrase implies the area associated with Ekron extended toward and reached the coastal zone.

paragraphs.title: The Hill Country: Shamir, Jattir and Dannah

easy.question: Which town appears at the start of verse 48?
easy.explanation: Shamir is named first among the mountain towns in verse 48.

easy.question: What type of content do verses 48–51 represent?
answers: a list of towns in the hill country
easy.explanation: The verses enumerate towns in the mountainous region — they are a place-list.

easy.question: Which trio appears together in verse 50?
easy.explanation: Verse 50 lists Anab, Eshtemoh and Anim together.

medium.question: What does the verse phrase 'which is Debir' (about Kiriath-sannah) indicate?
answers: that Kiriath-sannah is identical with Debir
that Debir is a river nearby
medium.explanation: The clause identifies Kiriath-sannah as the same place known also as Debir.

medium.question: In 'eleven cities with their villages' (v.49), what does 'their villages' mean?
answers: smaller settlements or farmsteads linked to the towns
medium.explanation: It refers to smaller dependent settlements around each main town.

medium.question: What does the opening word 'And in the mountains' imply about the location of the named towns?
answers: that they lie in a hill-country or mountainous area
that they have no fixed location
medium.explanation: It indicates these towns are located in the mountainous region rather than the plains.

challenge.question: Why does the author give 'eleven cities with their villages' instead of naming every small place?
answers: to show each city had associated rural settlements without listing them all
to imply each city had eleven public buildings
to suggest the cities were all empty
challenge.explanation: The summary form notes each principal town had surrounding villages, without enumerating every minor site.

challenge.question: Which geographical region do these towns most likely belong to?
challenge.explanation: Given the chapter's context and the phrase 'in the mountains', these towns are in Judah's hill country.

challenge.question: What does the sequence of names (Shamir, Jattir, Socoh, ...) suggest about how the compiler arranged the list?
answers: it is random with no discernible order
it likely follows local proximity or a known route
it follows a modern alphabetical order
challenge.explanation: Ancient lists often arrange place-names according to local geographic proximity or a travel route.

easy.question: Which of these names appears in verses 52–54?
easy.explanation: Beit Tappuah is listed in verse 53; Jerusalem and Shechem are not in this short list.

easy.question: How many cities are said to have their villages in verse 54?
easy.explanation: The verse ends with 'nine cities with their villages' — nine towns.

easy.question: What is the other name given for Kiriath-arba in the verse?
easy.explanation: The verse states 'Kiriath-arba is Hebron' — identifying the two as the same city.

medium.question: Why does the verse summarize with 'nine cities and their villages' after listing names?
answers: to indicate the total number of towns in that group
to add more towns not previously named
medium.explanation: The closing phrase tallies the number of towns in that subsection as nine, and notes their dependent villages.

medium.question: In 'nine cities and their villages', what does 'their villages' denote?
answers: dependent farms and small settlements around the towns
medium.explanation: It denotes the smaller settlements or agricultural hamlets associated with each town.

medium.question: Which place-name in verse 53 hints at a fruit in its name?
medium.explanation: 'Beit-Tappuah' literally contains 'tappuah' (apple/fruit), so the name hints at a fruit.

challenge.question: The text records the variant form '(Vinim) [Vinon]' next to a name. What does this indicate?
answers: different readings or manuscript variants of the same place-name
challenge.explanation: Bracketed variants usually signal different manuscript or textual traditions for the place-name.

challenge.question: Why does the author state 'Kiriath-arba is Hebron' rather than using only one name?
answers: to identify that Kiriath-arba and Hebron are the same place under two names
to indicate a ritual function only
challenge.explanation: The clause explicitly equates two names for the same city, aiding identification across traditions.

challenge.question: What broader historical point does identifying Kiriath-arba as Hebron suggest about place-names?
answers: that place-names could shift or coexist across time, showing continuity
that the city was newly founded at Joshua's time
that it was always a coastal settlement
challenge.explanation: It demonstrates that towns often had multiple names over time or in different traditions, indicating continuity of settlement.

paragraphs.title: Maon, Carmel and the Township Lists

easy.question: What do verses 55–56 list?
easy.explanation: These verses list place-names — towns and their villages.

easy.question: How many towns are noted in verse 57?
easy.explanation: Verse 57 states 'ten cities' — it lists ten towns.

easy.question: Which name appears in these verses?
easy.explanation: Maon is named in verse 55; Jericho and Megiddo are not in this section.

medium.question: What do all the names in verses 55–56 have in common?
answers: they are towns in Judah's territory
medium.explanation: They are all place-names — towns and villages within Judah's allotment.

medium.question: In 'ten cities and their villages' (v.57), what does 'their villages' imply?
answers: dependent rural settlements around the towns
the number of inhabitants in each city
medium.explanation: It indicates smaller hamlets and agricultural sites associated with each town.

medium.question: What does verse 57 do after listing names in 55–56?
answers: gives a count and notes the towns have villages
medium.explanation: It summarizes the list by counting ten towns and indicating each has associated villages.

challenge.question: How many town names are explicitly listed across verses 55–57?
challenge.explanation: Verses 55–56 list ten place-names in total for that subsection.

challenge.question: What geographic inference can be made about these towns?
answers: they are in the hill country of Judah
they lie in the northern Jordan valley
challenge.explanation: Given the chapter and context, these towns are associated with Judah's hill-country regions.

challenge.question: Why might a modern reader incorrectly assume the 'Jezreel' named here refers only to the famous northern Jezreel valley?
